newsitem.title: GERMANY: Snapshot-Bundesbank to discuss revaluation plan.
newsitem.headline: Snapshot-Bundesbank to discuss revaluation plan.

text.p: The Bundesbank will discuss a proposal from German Finance Minister Theo Waigel to revalue the central bank's gold and foreign exchange assets at a regular meeting on Wednesday.

Since the plan, which has still not been released in detail, was first mooted two weeks ago, it has drawn a plethora of official comment both within Germany and abroad, with some suggesting that it is a bid to improve the look of state finances.
Germany's reserves are valued according to the lowest price principle. Most other central banks in Europe already value their assets closer to the market price.
There is general agreement on the need to revalue any assets before they are transferred to the European Central Bank at the start of Europe's monetary union.
But confusion remains on how exactly the move will benefit Bonn's finances as it struggles to cut its deficit back to three percent of gross domestic product for EMU entry.
Following is a selection of the comments.

FRANKFURT, May 15 - Bundesbank statement: "With respect to the principles envisioned for accounting within the European System of Central Banks, Finance Minister Theo Waigel and State Secretary Juergen Stark presented initial thoughts on changes to some definitions on accounting principles in the Bundesbank law and conducted an initial exchange of views with the members of the central bank council at the meeting. The central bank council's discussions will be continued soon on the basis of a draft paper which will be drawn up by the German Finance Ministry."
BONN, May 15 - Finance ministry says tax revenues for 1997 will be 18 billion marks lower than expected.

BONN, May 15 - Waigel at news conference: "Germany will not sell one ounce of gold or one single dollar from the foreign exchange reserves...In preparation for monetary union it is necessary to put the accounting procedures of the Bundesbank on a new basis...The future valuation should take place at prices close to market levels".
FRANKFURT, May 16 - Bundesbank spokesman: "We have no further comments beyond what we said on Thursday".

BONN, May 16 - Waigel: "We will not go over three percent (ratio of deficit to gross domestic product....(It is) right and proper (to use Bundesbank gold reserves to offset old debt)...This is not a trick but normal practice".

BONN, May 16 - Opposition SPD finance expert Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier: "With an arrogant style Waigel has accused other European countries of manipulating their budgets to meet the Maastricht criteria...Now he is pulling the same stunt."

NEWSPAPERS, May 16 - Handelsblatt: "The budget fever of the last days is shameful for a state of the economic ranking of Germany. Mass cirulation Bild: "The Waigel miracle -- a billion-mark hole disappears overnight. Die Welt: "The plan hurts confidence in the stability structure (of Germany)."

ITALY, May 16 - Italian foreign minister Lamberto Dini tells International Herald Tribune newspaper: "I would be very surprised if the German government were to have recourse to accounting gimmicks such as the use of asset sales or a revaluation in order to meet a revenue shortfall for 1997."

BONN, May 16 - Chancellor Helmut Kohl commenting in parliament on Germany's problems in reining in spending, "We need a moment to contemplate. In July we will set out a new budget outline. At that point it will be decided whether we need a supplementary budget. But you can't expect us to give you answers today that we don't have."

BONN, May 18 - Germany's leading economic institutes criticise gold plan in leading newspapers. Heiner Flassbeck, director of IW institute in Berlin: "It is unsolid. It is also embarrassing in front of other Europeans".

FRANKFURT, May 19 - Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister in speech for delivery in Buenes Aires: "One will now watch very closely to see with what measures the financing deficit will be countered." No direct comment on gold plan.
BERLIN, May 20 - Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher: "Germany must fulfil the three percent (ratio) in 1997". No direct comment on gold revaluation plan.

PARIS, May 20 - Kohl tells news conference: "Upon reunification, the Federal Republic took on heavy debts which we have to bear...If we reach a certain agreement (on gold revaluation) we would put money into this (solidarity) fund to pay off these debts.

MAINZ, Germany, May 21 - Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick: "I cannot see at present how Germany can meet the decicit criterion without tricks in 1999." Says timing of announcement of gold revaluation plan unfortunate as it coincided with the poor tax estmiate figure.
BRUSSELS, May 21 - Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto: "It is not at all clear that one could accept that kind of manoeuvre. I think there is a question mark if they are talking about deficits."

LEIPZIG, May 22 - Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert: "As far as we are aware, Waigel plans to use these returns to retire more debt. Such a procedure would affect deficit and debt criteria (as the profits could be treated like tax income)...I am confident that the three percent goal can be reached in a manner which fully complies with the rules."
BRUSSELS, May 22 - Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt: "I don't see how it is possible to translate the revaluation to a reduction in public deficits."

AMSTERDAM, May 22 - Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm tells newspaper NRC Handelsblad: "It makes me worried that these kind of measures are being considered...Germany must meet the criteria in a proper manner. I can't imagine that Germany is prepared to put its reputation for soundness in the balance."

LONDON, May 23 - Former Bundesbank council member Wilhelm Noelling says the central bank should not succumb to government pressure to revalue its reserves. "It is not in the hand of Germany to safeguard the deutschemark...even if that means that Germany eventually fails to qualify for EMU entry in 1999."
REGENSBURG, Germany, May 24 - Waigel: "We are in a position, independent of the question of revaluing the gold reserves, to meet the Maastricht criteria".

PARIS, May 26 - German economics minister Guenter Rexrodt, on gold revaluation plan: "It is possible this year, but that depends on an assessment from the Bundesbank. My opinion is that we can proceed and we should proceed. There is space for such a revaluation and it is a serious measure."

DUESSELDORF, Germany, May 26 - Waigel: "The reorganisation of the accounts of the Bundesbank will be undertaken with the required caution. The financial solidity of the Bundesbank will be maintained...Taking over the accounting principles seen for the ECB is sensible."

HELSINKI, May 26 - Dutch central bank head Wim Duisenberg tells Finland's daily Helsingin Sanomat that the German revaluation plan is "not a trick". Says he expects reserves to be revalued to 70 percent of average value over last three years, the method used by the Dutch central bank.
--Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525
